newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS-Mexico's trade surplus seen dwindling.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Mexico's trade surplus seen dwindling.

text.p: A growing taste for imported goods caused Mexico's trade surplus to narrow quickly at the end of last year, a trend some fear may lead to the country's first trade deficits since the peso crash.
Exports outpaced imports by only $220 million in December, according to preliminary trade data released by the Commerce Ministry on Thursday.
Although that figure could be revised upwards, it showed a steady fall from trade surpluses of $254 million in November and October and $683 million in September.
The figure also fell well short of an expected December surplus of some $300 million in a Reuters' survey of Mexican economists MXAAP.

For the year, Mexico's trade figures looked good. It racked up a $6.292 billion preliminary surplus -- its second year of surpluses after whopping trade shortfalls in previous years that forced Mexico to borrow heavily and led in part to the 1994-1995 crisis.
But the shrinking surpluses have led to worries Mexico is once again returning to chronic trade deficits that it will find difficult to finance.

Economists said the country's trade surplus may not last much longer as the economy recovers from recession and companies import increasing amounts of goods, either as inputs for export or for sale in the domestic market.
"People are going to be surprised by how quickly the trade surplus falls," said Damian Fraser, the director of analysis at Caspian Research in Mexico City.
"In the past, imports have been very sensitive to domestic demand and economic growth...a combination of higher demand for consumer goods and intermediate goods," he said.
Fraser predicted Mexico will run a trade surplus of about $1 billion in 1997, with small monthly deficits appearing by mid-year. Other economists expect a 1997 surplus closer to $2 or $3 billion.
"I think that at the end of 1997, it (the trade surplus) will be $2.0 billion, which is one-third of what we had in 1996," said ING Barings economist Sergio Martin.
Martin said the December figures will prompt economists to lower their estimates for a 1997 trade surplus.
Despite the growing worries about a return to trade deficits, many economists agree Mexico can afford to finance a small trade shortfall.
"I think this is welcome. It shows the economy is growing and in no way is it a sign Mexico is returning to its bad old ways," said Carlos Rosales, head of economic research at Bancomer bank.
Rosales said Mexico's current account deficit, a measure of the country's balance of payments, stands at about 1.3 percent of GDP, low by international standards.

And the difference this time around compared to 1994 may be the peso itself, which is free-floating instead of fixed at an overvalued rate that makes imports artificially cheap, according to economists.

The peso has been gaining strength for much of the past year in real terms. As soon as red ink appears on trade numbers, however, investors are likely to push the currency lower, making Mexican exports cheaper and helping to correct the trade imbalance.
"It should be automatically adjusting. The peso may not weaken until people see a trade deficit," Fraser said.
Rosales said the Banco de Mexico has been sending signals to the currency market that it will allow a slightly weaker peso by not keeping interest rates at artificially high levels.
